evidence.exact_content: When I picture being 25, I hope I still play or run because I like being part of a team and testing myself, but I do not need sport to become my job. I want a small circle of friends I can be honest with, a lot of time outside, and work that helps restore trails or habitats. I am not sure whether that means environmental science, landscape design, or something I have not seen yet. The part I am sure about is that I want my work to leave a place better and my life to have room for people, not only achievements.
evidence.question_context: When you picture the life you want to build, what matters most to you — in sport, school or work, relationships, and who you want to become?

evidence.exact_content: Right now I want to become someone teammates trust in close moments without losing why I enjoy playing. For me that includes reading the field earlier, speaking clearly, and staying involved after a mistake instead of trying to erase it immediately. It matters because the best games feel shared rather than like a test I am taking alone. I would like to compete in college if the right chance is there, but I do not want that possibility to turn every practice into a judgment about my future.
evidence.question_context: What do you want from your sport right now, and why does that matter to you?

evidence.exact_content: My coach and family care about it, but this is a direction I chose. | Mine
evidence.question_context: Thinking about the sport goal you just described, whose goal does it feel like?

evidence.exact_content: Before a weekend tournament, I wrote down the three things I wanted ready before I went to sleep: my gear, food for the drive, and the address. I packed the gear and food myself and put the address in my phone. My parent chose when we left and drove. Rain moved our first game to another field after we were already on the road. I felt the rush come back, but I still had the things I had prepared. We reached the new field before warm-up ended. I can describe the sequence, but I cannot separate what mattered most to the timing.
evidence.question_context: Think of a practice or competition that mattered to you. What did you do to get ready, and which parts were your choice?

evidence.exact_content: I meant to finish the graphs for a science presentation on Wednesday. My lab partner sent the final measurements later than we expected, and I had a work shift that evening. I finished the written explanation, messaged my partner about which measurements were final, and made the graphs Thursday morning. We submitted on time, but I noticed an old unit label during our last check and we corrected it before presenting. I followed through, though not in the order I planned. The late measurements and my own decision to leave the graphs until I had them both shaped what happened.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about something you meant to follow through on recently. What happened when it was time to do it?

evidence.exact_content: At a trail-restoration volunteer day, I had to use a mapping app I had never seen. The coordinator demonstrated the whole process once, but I lost track after the first screen. I tried a sample entry, showed her exactly where I got stuck, and asked her to repeat only that part. I wrote a three-step note in my own words. On the next plot I entered the location without help. I still could not tell which plant condition to choose, so I left that field blank and asked instead of pretending I knew.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you were learning something unfamiliar. What helped you understand it, and what was still difficult?

evidence.exact_content: In practice, my coach told me to scan earlier before the ball arrived. At first I heard that as 'play faster,' which made me hurry. I asked what he would actually see if I did it well. He said he wanted one look over my shoulder before the pass came. I tried that in three possessions: once I saw the far-side option, once I looked but lost my first touch, and once the ball went somewhere else. The concrete cue made more sense than the first wording, but three possessions are not enough to tell me how dependable it will be.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about some feedback you received. What did you make of it, and what happened next?

evidence.exact_content: Late in a close game, I started giving teammates several instructions at once because I was trying to solve everything quickly. One teammate said, 'Give me one thing, not three.' At the next stoppage I used her name and said only which space I was covering. On the next play she pointed, and we moved in the same direction. I felt more settled, but I do not know whether the shorter message caused that play to work or whether the situation was simply clearer.
evidence.question_context: Think of a moment when you felt under pressure. What, if anything, changed in what you noticed or how you chose what to do next?

evidence.exact_content: During exam week I had two practices, a Saturday work shift, and a history paper due Friday. I wrote the fixed times down first, then told my coach I could attend practice but not the optional film session. I did shorter study blocks before each practice and kept the work shift because I had already agreed to it. The paper was submitted on time and I attended both practices. I was tired on Friday and did not do the extra run I had considered. I would make the same priority choice again, but I would start the paper earlier if I had another week like that.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a week when sport and school — or other responsibilities — were both demanding. How did you decide what got your time and attention, and how did it go?

evidence.exact_content: At a community clean-up, the volunteer leader was helping another group and our supplies were still in one pile. No one told me to do anything. I read the labels, made three small piles, and asked the people near me whether they wanted gloves, bags, or grabbers. Two people started from those piles and one person waited for the leader. When the leader returned, I asked whether the setup was okay; she moved one pile and kept the rest. I was comfortable starting something reversible, but I still wanted her decision on the final layout.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you chose what to do without a coach, parent or teammate telling you. What did you do?

evidence.exact_content: A teammate and I both thought the other person was assigning who would take our first set pieces. She said, 'I thought you had all of them.' I told her I was ready to take the first two but did not want to decide the rest without her. She said she wanted the next two, so we wrote our initials beside each one on the board. During the game the order changed after a substitution, and we checked with each other again. The conversation did not settle every future game; it gave us a shared plan for that one.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you worked something out with another person. What did you do, what did they actually say or do, and how did it go?

evidence.exact_content: I was not chosen to start a game after I had expected to. I felt embarrassed and my first thought was to stay quiet so nobody could tell. After warm-up I asked the coach for one thing to watch from the sideline. He said to notice when the other team left space behind their outside player. I wrote down two moments and stayed ready. I played later, but I do not know whether the note-taking affected that decision. What helped emotionally was having something real to pay attention to instead of replaying the lineup in my head.
evidence.question_context: Think of a time something was hard or didn't go your way. What did you do next, and what helped — if anything?

evidence.exact_content: A short checklist is working for me when several practical things have to happen. At the tournament, it helped me remember the gear, food, and address even after the field changed. The same habit can get in my way when I treat the list as more current than the people around me. At another practice I kept checking an old meeting spot while teammates were already moving inside because of weather. A teammate said, 'We are in the gym now,' and I had to stop looking at the list and look at what had changed.
evidence.question_context: What is working for you that you would like to keep? Tell me about a recent time it helped. If that same strength or habit has ever got in your way, you can include that too.

evidence.exact_content: I usually think I need time to prepare before I say something important. During a class discussion, the teacher asked a question I had not rehearsed. I said which part I was sure about, admitted which part I was not sure about, and connected it to an example from our reading. I did not have a polished answer, but the discussion kept moving and another student added to it. That moment does not mean I am suddenly comfortable speaking without preparation. It showed me I can contribute before everything is finished in my head.
evidence.question_context: Has something changed recently, or have you had a moment that doesn't fit the usual story about you? Tell me about it.

evidence.exact_content: People sometimes call me quiet and assume I am not competitive. From my side, I am usually trying to see the shape of what is happening before I speak. That can be useful, but it can also leave people without the information in my head. In the close game I went too far the other way and gave three instructions at once. I do not think 'quiet' or 'loud leader' fits. I am still learning how to say the one thing another person can actually use.
evidence.question_context: What is something people sometimes get wrong about you — or a label that does not fit? What would they understand better if they saw the situation from your side?

evidence.exact_content: I want the next step to help me communicate one useful thing without trying to control the whole moment. | Think about one small next step
evidence.question_context: What would be useful to you next?

human_realization.customer_prose:
## Written records repeat; scanning and unrehearsed speaking remain open

The strongest pattern here is not that writing guarantees a result. It is that you repeatedly choose a short written record when concrete details need holding: the tournament checklist, your three-step mapping note, fixed times during exam week, set-piece initials, and two sideline observations. Those are five separate situations, so this reading can confidently say the approach repeats. Even then, its usefulness is not automatic: you also described an old meeting-place list competing with teammates’ updated information. The careful interpretation is that writing serves you best when it stays connected to what is current.

Two other possibilities have much less evidence. You understand scanning as one look over your shoulder before the pass, but the test here is only three possessions in one practice, with different results. That shows understanding, not yet dependable execution.

Likewise, the class discussion matters because you contributed without a polished answer, despite usually expecting preparation. It is one real counterexample—not proof that unrehearsed speaking is now comfortable or consistent.

Every example came from your account, without outside confirmation. More attempts across different situations could strengthen—or revise—this picture.

sourceMoments.question: When you picture the life you want to build, what matters most to you — in sport, school or work, relationships, and who you want to become?
sourceMoments.answer: When I picture being 25, I hope I still play or run because I like being part of a team and testing myself, but I do not need sport to become my job. I want a small circle of friends I can be honest with, a lot of time outside, and work that helps restore trails or habitats. I am not sure whether that means environmental science, landscape design, or something I have not seen yet. The part I am sure about is that I want my work to leave a place better and my life to have room for people, not only achievements.

sourceMoments.question: What do you want from your sport right now, and why does that matter to you?
sourceMoments.answer: Right now I want to become someone teammates trust in close moments without losing why I enjoy playing. For me that includes reading the field earlier, speaking clearly, and staying involved after a mistake instead of trying to erase it immediately. It matters because the best games feel shared rather than like a test I am taking alone. I would like to compete in college if the right chance is there, but I do not want that possibility to turn every practice into a judgment about my future.

sourceMoments.question: Thinking about the sport goal you just described, whose goal does it feel like?
sourceMoments.answer: My coach and family care about it, but this is a direction I chose. | Mine

sourceMoments.question: Think of a practice or competition that mattered to you. What did you do to get ready, and which parts were your choice?
sourceMoments.answer: Before a weekend tournament, I wrote down the three things I wanted ready before I went to sleep: my gear, food for the drive, and the address. I packed the gear and food myself and put the address in my phone. My parent chose when we left and drove. Rain moved our first game to another field after we were already on the road. I felt the rush come back, but I still had the things I had prepared. We reached the new field before warm-up ended. I can describe the sequence, but I cannot separate what mattered most to the timing.

sourceMoments.question: Tell me about something you meant to follow through on recently. What happened when it was time to do it?
sourceMoments.answer: I meant to finish the graphs for a science presentation on Wednesday. My lab partner sent the final measurements later than we expected, and I had a work shift that evening. I finished the written explanation, messaged my partner about which measurements were final, and made the graphs Thursday morning. We submitted on time, but I noticed an old unit label during our last check and we corrected it before presenting. I followed through, though not in the order I planned. The late measurements and my own decision to leave the graphs until I had them both shaped what happened.

sourceMoments.question: Tell me about a time you were learning something unfamiliar. What helped you understand it, and what was still difficult?
sourceMoments.answer: At a trail-restoration volunteer day, I had to use a mapping app I had never seen. The coordinator demonstrated the whole process once, but I lost track after the first screen. I tried a sample entry, showed her exactly where I got stuck, and asked her to repeat only that part. I wrote a three-step note in my own words. On the next plot I entered the location without help. I still could not tell which plant condition to choose, so I left that field blank and asked instead of pretending I knew.

sourceMoments.question: Tell me about some feedback you received. What did you make of it, and what happened next?
sourceMoments.answer: In practice, my coach told me to scan earlier before the ball arrived. At first I heard that as 'play faster,' which made me hurry. I asked what he would actually see if I did it well. He said he wanted one look over my shoulder before the pass came. I tried that in three possessions: once I saw the far-side option, once I looked but lost my first touch, and once the ball went somewhere else. The concrete cue made more sense than the first wording, but three possessions are not enough to tell me how dependable it will be.

sourceMoments.question: Think of a moment when you felt under pressure. What, if anything, changed in what you noticed or how you chose what to do next?
sourceMoments.answer: Late in a close game, I started giving teammates several instructions at once because I was trying to solve everything quickly. One teammate said, 'Give me one thing, not three.' At the next stoppage I used her name and said only which space I was covering. On the next play she pointed, and we moved in the same direction. I felt more settled, but I do not know whether the shorter message caused that play to work or whether the situation was simply clearer.

sourceMoments.question: Tell me about a week when sport and school — or other responsibilities — were both demanding. How did you decide what got your time and attention, and how did it go?
sourceMoments.answer: During exam week I had two practices, a Saturday work shift, and a history paper due Friday. I wrote the fixed times down first, then told my coach I could attend practice but not the optional film session. I did shorter study blocks before each practice and kept the work shift because I had already agreed to it. The paper was submitted on time and I attended both practices. I was tired on Friday and did not do the extra run I had considered. I would make the same priority choice again, but I would start the paper earlier if I had another week like that.

sourceMoments.question: Tell me about a time you chose what to do without a coach, parent or teammate telling you. What did you do?
sourceMoments.answer: At a community clean-up, the volunteer leader was helping another group and our supplies were still in one pile. No one told me to do anything. I read the labels, made three small piles, and asked the people near me whether they wanted gloves, bags, or grabbers. Two people started from those piles and one person waited for the leader. When the leader returned, I asked whether the setup was okay; she moved one pile and kept the rest. I was comfortable starting something reversible, but I still wanted her decision on the final layout.

sourceMoments.question: Tell me about a time you worked something out with another person. What did you do, what did they actually say or do, and how did it go?
sourceMoments.answer: A teammate and I both thought the other person was assigning who would take our first set pieces. She said, 'I thought you had all of them.' I told her I was ready to take the first two but did not want to decide the rest without her. She said she wanted the next two, so we wrote our initials beside each one on the board. During the game the order changed after a substitution, and we checked with each other again. The conversation did not settle every future game; it gave us a shared plan for that one.

sourceMoments.question: Think of a time something was hard or didn't go your way. What did you do next, and what helped — if anything?
sourceMoments.answer: I was not chosen to start a game after I had expected to. I felt embarrassed and my first thought was to stay quiet so nobody could tell. After warm-up I asked the coach for one thing to watch from the sideline. He said to notice when the other team left space behind their outside player. I wrote down two moments and stayed ready. I played later, but I do not know whether the note-taking affected that decision. What helped emotionally was having something real to pay attention to instead of replaying the lineup in my head.

sourceMoments.question: What is working for you that you would like to keep? Tell me about a recent time it helped. If that same strength or habit has ever got in your way, you can include that too.
sourceMoments.answer: A short checklist is working for me when several practical things have to happen. At the tournament, it helped me remember the gear, food, and address even after the field changed. The same habit can get in my way when I treat the list as more current than the people around me. At another practice I kept checking an old meeting spot while teammates were already moving inside because of weather. A teammate said, 'We are in the gym now,' and I had to stop looking at the list and look at what had changed.

sourceMoments.question: Has something changed recently, or have you had a moment that doesn't fit the usual story about you? Tell me about it.
sourceMoments.answer: I usually think I need time to prepare before I say something important. During a class discussion, the teacher asked a question I had not rehearsed. I said which part I was sure about, admitted which part I was not sure about, and connected it to an example from our reading. I did not have a polished answer, but the discussion kept moving and another student added to it. That moment does not mean I am suddenly comfortable speaking without preparation. It showed me I can contribute before everything is finished in my head.

sourceMoments.question: For the moment you want MORE to understand best, were the conditions usual for you?
sourceMoments.answer: It was a higher-pressure game than most of our practices. | Something was different

sourceMoments.question: For the task you named, how sure do you feel about doing it right now?
sourceMoments.answer: I understand the cue now, but I have only tested it a few times. | Fairly sure

sourceMoments.question: How much room do you have for anything extra right now?
sourceMoments.answer: I have room for one small thing, not another full schedule. | Some

sourceMoments.question: Is there any support you need, or a limit MORE should respect, when thinking about next steps?
sourceMoments.answer: School and my Saturday work shift need to stay in the plan. | time or other responsibilities

sourceMoments.question: What is something people sometimes get wrong about you — or a label that does not fit? What would they understand better if they saw the situation from your side?
sourceMoments.answer: People sometimes call me quiet and assume I am not competitive. From my side, I am usually trying to see the shape of what is happening before I speak. That can be useful, but it can also leave people without the information in my head. In the close game I went too far the other way and gave three instructions at once. I do not think 'quiet' or 'loud leader' fits. I am still learning how to say the one thing another person can actually use.

sourceMoments.question: What would be useful to you next?
sourceMoments.answer: I want the next step to help me communicate one useful thing without trying to control the whole moment. | Think about one small next step

Mika was comfortable starting a reversible clean-up setup but wanted the leader’s decision on the final layout.
After not starting, Mika’s first thought was to hide the embarrassment.
Mika usually thinks important speaking requires preparation, but now has one counterexample.
whole_person_model.pressure_and_recovery: Two episodes give different, limited pictures. In the higher-pressure game, Mika initially bundled instructions and then shortened the message after teammate input. After not starting, a concrete observation target helped emotionally. Current responses after mistakes and broader recovery methods remain undescribed.
whole_person_model.work_and_relationships: Mika hopes for honest friendships, time outdoors, and work restoring trails or habitats, although the exact occupation remains open. Current school and Saturday work responsibilities must remain in the plan. One teammate interaction produced a shared plan for one game, and one clean-up interaction showed reversible initiative while leaving the final arrangement with the leader.
whole_person_model.identity_distillation: Mika is better understood here as someone learning to turn observation and competitiveness into one timely, usable contribution—not as a fixed leadership type. Sport matters, but it sits within a larger hoped-for life centered on people, outdoor places, and meaningful work. This understanding remains open to correction.

evidence.exact_content: When I picture being 25, I hope I still play or run because I like being part of a team and testing myself, but I do not need sport to become my job. I want a small circle of friends I can be honest with, a lot of time outside, and work that helps restore trails or habitats. I am not sure whether that means environmental science, landscape design, or something I have not seen yet. The part I am sure about is that I want my work to leave a place better and my life to have room for people, not only achievements.
evidence.question_context: When you picture the life you want to build, what matters most to you — in sport, school or work, relationships, and who you want to become?

evidence.exact_content: Right now I want to become someone teammates trust in close moments without losing why I enjoy playing. For me that includes reading the field earlier, speaking clearly, and staying involved after a mistake instead of trying to erase it immediately. It matters because the best games feel shared rather than like a test I am taking alone. I would like to compete in college if the right chance is there, but I do not want that possibility to turn every practice into a judgment about my future.
evidence.question_context: What do you want from your sport right now, and why does that matter to you?

evidence.exact_content: My coach and family care about it, but this is a direction I chose. | Mine
evidence.question_context: Thinking about the sport goal you just described, whose goal does it feel like?

evidence.exact_content: Before a weekend tournament, I wrote down the three things I wanted ready before I went to sleep: my gear, food for the drive, and the address. I packed the gear and food myself and put the address in my phone. My parent chose when we left and drove. Rain moved our first game to another field after we were already on the road. I felt the rush come back, but I still had the things I had prepared. We reached the new field before warm-up ended. I can describe the sequence, but I cannot separate what mattered most to the timing.
evidence.question_context: Think of a practice or competition that mattered to you. What did you do to get ready, and which parts were your choice?

evidence.exact_content: I meant to finish the graphs for a science presentation on Wednesday. My lab partner sent the final measurements later than we expected, and I had a work shift that evening. I finished the written explanation, messaged my partner about which measurements were final, and made the graphs Thursday morning. We submitted on time, but I noticed an old unit label during our last check and we corrected it before presenting. I followed through, though not in the order I planned. The late measurements and my own decision to leave the graphs until I had them both shaped what happened.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about something you meant to follow through on recently. What happened when it was time to do it?

evidence.exact_content: At a trail-restoration volunteer day, I had to use a mapping app I had never seen. The coordinator demonstrated the whole process once, but I lost track after the first screen. I tried a sample entry, showed her exactly where I got stuck, and asked her to repeat only that part. I wrote a three-step note in my own words. On the next plot I entered the location without help. I still could not tell which plant condition to choose, so I left that field blank and asked instead of pretending I knew.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you were learning something unfamiliar. What helped you understand it, and what was still difficult?

evidence.exact_content: In practice, my coach told me to scan earlier before the ball arrived. At first I heard that as 'play faster,' which made me hurry. I asked what he would actually see if I did it well. He said he wanted one look over my shoulder before the pass came. I tried that in three possessions: once I saw the far-side option, once I looked but lost my first touch, and once the ball went somewhere else. The concrete cue made more sense than the first wording, but three possessions are not enough to tell me how dependable it will be.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about some feedback you received. What did you make of it, and what happened next?

evidence.exact_content: Late in a close game, I started giving teammates several instructions at once because I was trying to solve everything quickly. One teammate said, 'Give me one thing, not three.' At the next stoppage I used her name and said only which space I was covering. On the next play she pointed, and we moved in the same direction. I felt more settled, but I do not know whether the shorter message caused that play to work or whether the situation was simply clearer.
evidence.question_context: Think of a moment when you felt under pressure. What, if anything, changed in what you noticed or how you chose what to do next?

evidence.exact_content: During exam week I had two practices, a Saturday work shift, and a history paper due Friday. I wrote the fixed times down first, then told my coach I could attend practice but not the optional film session. I did shorter study blocks before each practice and kept the work shift because I had already agreed to it. The paper was submitted on time and I attended both practices. I was tired on Friday and did not do the extra run I had considered. I would make the same priority choice again, but I would start the paper earlier if I had another week like that.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a week when sport and school — or other responsibilities — were both demanding. How did you decide what got your time and attention, and how did it go?

evidence.exact_content: At a community clean-up, the volunteer leader was helping another group and our supplies were still in one pile. No one told me to do anything. I read the labels, made three small piles, and asked the people near me whether they wanted gloves, bags, or grabbers. Two people started from those piles and one person waited for the leader. When the leader returned, I asked whether the setup was okay; she moved one pile and kept the rest. I was comfortable starting something reversible, but I still wanted her decision on the final layout.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you chose what to do without a coach, parent or teammate telling you. What did you do?

evidence.exact_content: A teammate and I both thought the other person was assigning who would take our first set pieces. She said, 'I thought you had all of them.' I told her I was ready to take the first two but did not want to decide the rest without her. She said she wanted the next two, so we wrote our initials beside each one on the board. During the game the order changed after a substitution, and we checked with each other again. The conversation did not settle every future game; it gave us a shared plan for that one.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you worked something out with another person. What did you do, what did they actually say or do, and how did it go?

evidence.exact_content: I was not chosen to start a game after I had expected to. I felt embarrassed and my first thought was to stay quiet so nobody could tell. After warm-up I asked the coach for one thing to watch from the sideline. He said to notice when the other team left space behind their outside player. I wrote down two moments and stayed ready. I played later, but I do not know whether the note-taking affected that decision. What helped emotionally was having something real to pay attention to instead of replaying the lineup in my head.
evidence.question_context: Think of a time something was hard or didn't go your way. What did you do next, and what helped — if anything?

evidence.exact_content: A short checklist is working for me when several practical things have to happen. At the tournament, it helped me remember the gear, food, and address even after the field changed. The same habit can get in my way when I treat the list as more current than the people around me. At another practice I kept checking an old meeting spot while teammates were already moving inside because of weather. A teammate said, 'We are in the gym now,' and I had to stop looking at the list and look at what had changed.
evidence.question_context: What is working for you that you would like to keep? Tell me about a recent time it helped. If that same strength or habit has ever got in your way, you can include that too.

evidence.exact_content: I usually think I need time to prepare before I say something important. During a class discussion, the teacher asked a question I had not rehearsed. I said which part I was sure about, admitted which part I was not sure about, and connected it to an example from our reading. I did not have a polished answer, but the discussion kept moving and another student added to it. That moment does not mean I am suddenly comfortable speaking without preparation. It showed me I can contribute before everything is finished in my head.
evidence.question_context: Has something changed recently, or have you had a moment that doesn't fit the usual story about you? Tell me about it.

evidence.exact_content: It was a higher-pressure game than most of our practices. | Something was different
evidence.question_context: For the moment you want MORE to understand best, were the conditions usual for you?

evidence.exact_content: I understand the cue now, but I have only tested it a few times. | Fairly sure
evidence.question_context: For the task you named, how sure do you feel about doing it right now?

evidence.exact_content: I have room for one small thing, not another full schedule. | Some
evidence.question_context: How much room do you have for anything extra right now?

evidence.exact_content: School and my Saturday work shift need to stay in the plan. | time or other responsibilities
evidence.question_context: Is there any support you need, or a limit MORE should respect, when thinking about next steps?

evidence.exact_content: People sometimes call me quiet and assume I am not competitive. From my side, I am usually trying to see the shape of what is happening before I speak. That can be useful, but it can also leave people without the information in my head. In the close game I went too far the other way and gave three instructions at once. I do not think 'quiet' or 'loud leader' fits. I am still learning how to say the one thing another person can actually use.
evidence.question_context: What is something people sometimes get wrong about you — or a label that does not fit? What would they understand better if they saw the situation from your side?

evidence.exact_content: I want the next step to help me communicate one useful thing without trying to control the whole moment. | Think about one small next step
evidence.question_context: What would be useful to you next?

A short checklist helped with current practical details but got in the way when an old list competed with changed information. Mika identifies the difference as whether the list remained current.

evidence.question_context: When you picture the life you want to build, what matters most to you — in sport, school or work, relationships, and who you want to become?

evidence.text: Right now I want to become someone teammates trust in close moments without losing why I enjoy playing. For me that includes reading the field earlier, speaking clearly, and staying involved after a mistake instead of trying to erase it immediately. It matters because the best games feel shared rather than like a test I am taking alone. I would like to compete in college if the right chance is there, but I do not want that possibility to turn every practice into a judgment about my future.
evidence.question_context: What do you want from your sport right now, and why does that matter to you?

evidence.text: My coach and family care about it, but this is a direction I chose. | Mine
evidence.question_context: Thinking about the sport goal you just described, whose goal does it feel like?

evidence.text: Before a weekend tournament, I wrote down the three things I wanted ready before I went to sleep: my gear, food for the drive, and the address. I packed the gear and food myself and put the address in my phone. My parent chose when we left and drove. Rain moved our first game to another field after we were already on the road. I felt the rush come back, but I still had the things I had prepared. We reached the new field before warm-up ended. I can describe the sequence, but I cannot separate what mattered most to the timing.
evidence.question_context: Think of a practice or competition that mattered to you. What did you do to get ready, and which parts were your choice?

evidence.text: I meant to finish the graphs for a science presentation on Wednesday. My lab partner sent the final measurements later than we expected, and I had a work shift that evening. I finished the written explanation, messaged my partner about which measurements were final, and made the graphs Thursday morning. We submitted on time, but I noticed an old unit label during our last check and we corrected it before presenting. I followed through, though not in the order I planned. The late measurements and my own decision to leave the graphs until I had them both shaped what happened.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about something you meant to follow through on recently. What happened when it was time to do it?

evidence.text: At a trail-restoration volunteer day, I had to use a mapping app I had never seen. The coordinator demonstrated the whole process once, but I lost track after the first screen. I tried a sample entry, showed her exactly where I got stuck, and asked her to repeat only that part. I wrote a three-step note in my own words. On the next plot I entered the location without help. I still could not tell which plant condition to choose, so I left that field blank and asked instead of pretending I knew.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you were learning something unfamiliar. What helped you understand it, and what was still difficult?

evidence.text: In practice, my coach told me to scan earlier before the ball arrived. At first I heard that as 'play faster,' which made me hurry. I asked what he would actually see if I did it well. He said he wanted one look over my shoulder before the pass came. I tried that in three possessions: once I saw the far-side option, once I looked but lost my first touch, and once the ball went somewhere else. The concrete cue made more sense than the first wording, but three possessions are not enough to tell me how dependable it will be.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about some feedback you received. What did you make of it, and what happened next?

evidence.text: Late in a close game, I started giving teammates several instructions at once because I was trying to solve everything quickly. One teammate said, 'Give me one thing, not three.' At the next stoppage I used her name and said only which space I was covering. On the next play she pointed, and we moved in the same direction. I felt more settled, but I do not know whether the shorter message caused that play to work or whether the situation was simply clearer.
evidence.question_context: Think of a moment when you felt under pressure. What, if anything, changed in what you noticed or how you chose what to do next?

evidence.text: During exam week I had two practices, a Saturday work shift, and a history paper due Friday. I wrote the fixed times down first, then told my coach I could attend practice but not the optional film session. I did shorter study blocks before each practice and kept the work shift because I had already agreed to it. The paper was submitted on time and I attended both practices. I was tired on Friday and did not do the extra run I had considered. I would make the same priority choice again, but I would start the paper earlier if I had another week like that.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a week when sport and school — or other responsibilities — were both demanding. How did you decide what got your time and attention, and how did it go?

evidence.text: At a community clean-up, the volunteer leader was helping another group and our supplies were still in one pile. No one told me to do anything. I read the labels, made three small piles, and asked the people near me whether they wanted gloves, bags, or grabbers. Two people started from those piles and one person waited for the leader. When the leader returned, I asked whether the setup was okay; she moved one pile and kept the rest. I was comfortable starting something reversible, but I still wanted her decision on the final layout.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you chose what to do without a coach, parent or teammate telling you. What did you do?

evidence.text: A teammate and I both thought the other person was assigning who would take our first set pieces. She said, 'I thought you had all of them.' I told her I was ready to take the first two but did not want to decide the rest without her. She said she wanted the next two, so we wrote our initials beside each one on the board. During the game the order changed after a substitution, and we checked with each other again. The conversation did not settle every future game; it gave us a shared plan for that one.
evidence.question_context: Tell me about a time you worked something out with another person. What did you do, what did they actually say or do, and how did it go?

evidence.text: I was not chosen to start a game after I had expected to. I felt embarrassed and my first thought was to stay quiet so nobody could tell. After warm-up I asked the coach for one thing to watch from the sideline. He said to notice when the other team left space behind their outside player. I wrote down two moments and stayed ready. I played later, but I do not know whether the note-taking affected that decision. What helped emotionally was having something real to pay attention to instead of replaying the lineup in my head.
evidence.question_context: Think of a time something was hard or didn't go your way. What did you do next, and what helped — if anything?

evidence.text: A short checklist is working for me when several practical things have to happen. At the tournament, it helped me remember the gear, food, and address even after the field changed. The same habit can get in my way when I treat the list as more current than the people around me. At another practice I kept checking an old meeting spot while teammates were already moving inside because of weather. A teammate said, 'We are in the gym now,' and I had to stop looking at the list and look at what had changed.
evidence.question_context: What is working for you that you would like to keep? Tell me about a recent time it helped. If that same strength or habit has ever got in your way, you can include that too.

evidence.text: I usually think I need time to prepare before I say something important. During a class discussion, the teacher asked a question I had not rehearsed. I said which part I was sure about, admitted which part I was not sure about, and connected it to an example from our reading. I did not have a polished answer, but the discussion kept moving and another student added to it. That moment does not mean I am suddenly comfortable speaking without preparation. It showed me I can contribute before everything is finished in my head.
evidence.question_context: Has something changed recently, or have you had a moment that doesn't fit the usual story about you? Tell me about it.

evidence.text: It was a higher-pressure game than most of our practices. | Something was different

I felt more settled, but I do not know whether the shorter message caused that play to work or whether the situation was simply clearer.

evidence.text: People sometimes call me quiet and assume I am not competitive. From my side, I am usually trying to see the shape of what is happening before I speak. That can be useful, but it can also leave people without the information in my head. In the close game I went too far the other way and gave three instructions at once. I do not think 'quiet' or 'loud leader' fits. I am still learning how to say the one thing another person can actually use.
evidence.question_context: What is something people sometimes get wrong about you — or a label that does not fit? What would they understand better if they saw the situation from your side?

evidence.text: I want the next step to help me communicate one useful thing without trying to control the whole moment. | Think about one small next step
evidence.question_context: What would be useful to you next?
